articles.title: South Sudan - Key Message Update: Conflict, poor rainfall, and economic impacts drive Emergency and risk of Famine, July 2026 - January 2027
articles.description: Country: South Sudan Source: Famine Early Warning System Network Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes remain widespread as the lean season peaks in July and August, driven by conflict, insecurity, high inflation linked to a deteriorating macroeconomy, high food prices, and the impact of evolving drought conditions on household access to food and income.Humanitarian food assistance is expected to mitigate the severity of outcomes to Crisis! (IPC Phase 3!) through September in 12 counties in Jonglei, Unity, and Upper Nile.However, the fragile security environment and renewed armed clashes in Akobo, Nyirol, and eastern Uror are still limiting humanitarian access in remote locations. While the arrival of the main harvests in September and October will partially ease food consumption deficits through January, it will likely be insufficient to compensate for expected declines in food assistance, driving Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes across most of Jonglei, southern Upper Nile, and parts of Unity, Warrap, Lakes, and Northern Bahr el Ghazal. Akobo, Nyirol (Jonglei), Ulang, and Nasir (Upper Nile) remain in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) , with some households facing Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) . Access remains constrained, and a recent partner assessment in Akobo West found continuing food shortages, heavy reliance on wild foods, and a Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) rate by Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) of 22.3 percent, exceeding the Extremely Critical threshold (GAM-MUAC >15 percent). Severe outcomes are expected to persist through January 2027, as assistance declines while minimal harvests are likely due to the combined impacts of conflict, weather, and economic shocks. Akobo, Nyirol, Ulang, and Nasir counties will face a credible risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5) through January. Of particular concern are households in remote locations who have limited or no access to basic health services, have lost their livelihood assets, and are entirely reliant on wild foods and limited food assistance. If conflict re-escalates and is sustained at similar or higher levels than in early 2026 and isolates populations from accessing wild foods and food assistance for a prolonged period, then Famine (IPC Phase 5) would occur. Humanitarian food assistance remains critical in mitigating widening lean season consumption gaps . Despite the fragile security environment and funding shortfalls, WFP reached nearly 875,000 people with in-kind and cash assistance in June. Distributions are expected to mitigate more severe outcomes through September in Leer, Mayendit, Panyijiar, and Rubkona (Unity); Ayod, Duk, Canal/Pigi, Fangak, Uror, and Twic East (Jonglei); Pibor of Greater Pibor Administrative Area (GPAA); and Abyei Administrative Area (Abyei). After completing May and June distributions, July distributions are temporarily on hold in Duk following the deadly attack on a humanitarian convoy on June 29 and in Akobo West due to ongoing insecurity. Distributions in Baliet remain more permanently paused due to the past looting of assistance, with many households facing large food consumption gaps in July. In Nasir, FEWS NET confirmed distribution of a 21-day food ration per person provided to households in hard-to-reach areas of Kuerentngkee, Mandeng, Nyetot (Jikmir Payam ), Torkech, and Maker in mid-June, following the reopening of the Matar-Nasir humanitarian corridor. Partners are also scaling up cash and livelihood support assistance in Eastern Equatoria in response to the ongoing drought conditions. Conflict broke out again between government and opposition forces in July in parts of Jonglei and Upper Nile. The clashes were reported in Walgak (Akobo) on July 5, Panyikang on July 5, Waat (Uror) on July 6, Nasir on July 3 and 14, and Lankien (Nyirol) on July 13. These confrontations killed more than 100 people cumulatively, disrupted markets and crop production, constrained humanitarian access, and displaced at least 7,000 people. Additionally, SSPDF and UPDF forces clashed in Kajo-Keji on July 14 , displacing over 10,000 people . Intercommunal conflict related to cattle raiding and revenge also intensified. In Warrap, attacks between July 3-13 across Tonj North, Tonj South , Tonj East, and Twic caused 74 deaths, the loss of over 200 cattle, and displacement of 40,000 people. In Western Bahr el Ghazal, attacks in Jur River , Wau Town , and Raja killed 12 people, raided 40 cattle, and displaced 5,000 people . Strengthening El Niño conditions are driving below-average rainfall, soil water deficits , and poor crop growth conditions over much of the country . The rainfall deficits currently rank as the driest on historical record and are expected to remain below average for the season . Combined with above-average temperatures, these deficits are stressing crops and pasture conditions, as indicated by below-average vegetation health in Eastern Equatoria, northern Central Equatoria, Lakes, Unity, southern Jonglei, and northern Upper Nile. Key informants, field monitoring, and partner assessments have further confirmed germination failure, crop wilting, and delayed planting in parts of Upper Nile; Northern Bahr el Ghazal; Warrap; Mundri, Tambura, and Nagero (Western Equatoria); and the Kapoetas and Lopa/Lafon (Eastern Equatoria). While early above-average rainfall in February and March is sustaining relatively better pasture conditions and livestock health in central Jonglei and southern Upper Nile, pastures are more rapidly deteriorating in the pastoral region of the Kapoetas (Eastern Equatoria), leading to fair to poor livestock body conditions. Continued currency depreciation and rising fuel prices are driving elevated staple food prices amid low household purchasing power**.** Between June and July 2026, the price of fuel increased by 5-20 percent in Rumbek Centre, Wau, Aweil Centre, Bor South and Juba, and was 60-130 percent higher than in February 2026. Rising transport costs are aggravating seasonal price increases for staple foods. Based on available market price monitoring data , the price of red sorghum per malwa (3.5 kilograms) in June was 10-32 percent higher in Rumbek Centre, Rubkona, Gogrial East, and Aweil Centre markets. While July price data is not yet available, FEWS NET weekly monitoring of Juba prices found continued increases in the price of red sorghum, up 9 percent between the first and second weeks of July. In severely conflict-affected areas, price increases are particularly sharp as supplies decline and trade flows remain disrupted. For example, FEWS NET’s rapid market assessment in Nasir found the retail price of red sorghum rose by 43 percent between June and July.

articles.title: Zambia - Key Message Update: Stressed (IPC Phase 2) expected through January in Western and Southern provinces, July 2026 - January 2027
articles.description: Country: Zambia Source: Famine Early Warning System Network Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected from July to September in parts of the Western and Southern provinces and in localized areas in the east, driven by April flooding, localized production losses, prolonged dry spells, and Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD)-related livestock movement restrictions. Most households are expected to meet their minimum food needs from food stocks, non-agricultural labor, and livestock-related income. Households in the affected areas will have below-average purchasing power, which will continue to limit their ability to cover livelihood expenses. From October 2026 to January 2027, Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected to expand across the Western, Southern, Central, and Northern provinces as the lean season progresses. Households’ food stocks are expected to decline, and below-average agricultural labor income will further erode purchasing power. However, poor households are expected to meet their minimum food needs through market purchases, seasonal labor, and other livelihood activities. Minimal (IPC Phase 1) outcomes are expected to persist in the remaining parts of Zambia through January 2027, supported by above-average food stocks following the record 2026 harvest . Favorable national maize production has resulted in adequate household food availability and well-supplied markets, while declining staple food prices and improved terms of trade are expected to support food access for both farming and market-dependent households during much of the outlook period. However, as the lean season progresses, household food stocks are expected to decline gradually, increasing reliance on market purchases, particularly from October through January. Staple food prices continued to decline seasonally following the main harvest, supported by increased household stocks and improved market supplies. According to the Zambia Statistics Agency (ZAMSTAT) Monthly Bulletin , the national average retail price of maize grain declined by 12.5 percent between May and June 2026, while breakfast meal and roller meal prices fell by nearly 6 percent. Compared to June 2025, staple food prices remained lower in June 2026, supported by the record 2026 harvest and improved domestic market supplies. Above-average national maize supplies and planned Food Reserve Agency (FRA) procurement are expected to keep markets adequately supplied and support producers during the marketing season (August to October). Zambia's record harvest, combined with substantial carry-over stocks, is expected to ensure sufficient domestic maize availability, while the FRA's planned procurement of at least 500,000 metric tons will provide an important market for surplus-producing households. In July, gas and diesel pump prices declined by 3.7 percent and 12.5 percent, respectively, reflecting lower international oil prices and the continued appreciation of the ZMW. The reduction in fuel prices is expected to lower transport and distribution costs, helping drive the seasonal decline in staple food prices during the marketing season. However, the passthrough of lower fuel costs to food prices is expected to remain limited in remote and structurally deficit markets, particularly in parts of Western Province, where poor road infrastructure, high transport costs, and localized supply constraints continue to restrict market access.

articles.title: Madagascar - Key Message Update: An early lean season will erode limited seasonal gains in the Grand South, July 2026 - January 2027
articles.description: Country: Madagascar Source: Famine Early Warning System Network Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to emerge in Toliara II and Amboasary Atsimo in July as poor households exhaust food stocks atypically early following below-average production and become increasingly market dependent amid seasonal food price increases. From October 2026, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to expand across several areas of Atsimo-Andrefana and Androy and parts of Anosy as more households deplete their stocks and lack sufficient resources to meet their essential food and non-food needs. Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected to persist through September throughout the rest of the Grand South. Cassava and sweet potato harvests, concentrated between July and August, will temporarily support household food consumption and income from crop sales. However, production is expected to be significantly below average due to forecast below-average and erratic rainfall, which will limit the magnitude and duration of improvements provided by the harvests. The ongoing El Niño event is likely to result in a delayed onset of the upcoming October rainy season, above-average temperatures, and below-average rainfall. These forecast weather shocks are expected to hinder the establishment of key staple crops such as rice, maize, and cassava in the Grand South and Grand South East. Below-average crop production will reduce demand for agricultural labor, keeping labor earnings 20 to 40 percent below average. Amid limited household food stocks and reduced purchasing power, poor households will face widening food consumption gaps during the lean season and increasingly rely on borrowing, asset sales, temporary migration, and consumption of wild foods. Food prices will likely face additional upward pressure from rising international fuel, freight, and import costs. Although domestic fuel prices have remained broadly stable under the government's price adjustment mechanism and emergency subsidies, higher costs for imported fuel and essential commodities, partly associated with renewed tensions in the Middle East, are likely to increase food prices over the outlook period. Government price stabilization measures are unlikely to fully offset these pressures, further eroding poor households’ purchasing power and intensifying the effects of the lean season, particularly in the Grand South.
